section_summary: This section documents the State Department’s 1937 investigation of claims that as many as 100,000 Japanese lived in Mexico; consular returns instead produced an estimate of about 5,300, including roughly 1,650 in Baja California. Related reports describe Japanese fishing ventures on Mexico’s Pacific coast, agricultural colonies, migration patterns, local community organization, and possible propaganda or intelligence implications. Most of the section is an enclosed Spanish-language book, Keiichi Ito’s El alma del Japón, which celebrates Japanese culture and modernization while defending Japan’s policies in Manchuria and China and portraying the Soviet Union as the principal threat to peace in East Asia.

subfiles.title: Internal note on handling the War Department’s information request
subfiles.about: Records an internal discussion of responsibility for answering part of the War Department’s request and the confidentiality of ensuing consular instructions.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Tanis states that the Department can answer the fourth item in the War Department’s letter more quickly than the Consulate General and that arrangements have already been made. When the writer proposes adding an explicit secrecy warning, Tanis replies that the Consulate General will probably circulate the instruction only to consulates already accustomed to handling such matters confidentially.

subfiles.title: Instruction requesting statistics on Japanese residents and immigration in Mexico
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Thomas D. Bowman, American Consul General, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Requests a carefully prepared report on the number and recent immigration of Japanese in Mexico and Baja California.
subfiles.summary: The Department relays an April 29 War Department request for the number of Japanese in Mexico, the number in Baja California, and the number who had immigrated during the preceding two years. Bowman is authorized to enlist every American consular officer in Mexico to obtain complete and accurate information.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 275 concerning the Japanese situation in Mexico and Central America
subfiles.from: Fay Allen Des Portes, American Legation, Guatemala
subfiles.about: Reports President Jorge Ubico’s concerns about the scale and strategic significance of Japanese activity in Mexico and along the Pacific coast.
subfiles.summary: During a conversation, President Ubico asserts that more than 100,000 Japanese live in Mexico and that Japanese fishing vessels are active along the Pacific coast from Panama through Mexico. Although he believes Japan is heavily occupied in China, he regards the situation in the Americas as critical and links it to the security of the United States and Central America.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 43: Information for War Department regarding number of Japanese in Mexico
subfiles.from: James B. Stewart, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Explains that the requested population report is being delayed pending William A. Smale’s field investigation in northern Baja California.
subfiles.summary: Stewart refers to the May 4 instruction and reports that Consul William A. Smale is conducting a personal investigation of Japanese residents in northern Baja California. Smale planned to visit several locations and complete the trip by the end of June, with his expenses paid by the War Department; Stewart promises an immediate report once Smale’s findings arrive.

subfiles.title: Japanese living in the Durango Consular District
subfiles.from: E. E. Eaton, American Vice Consul, Durango
subfiles.about: Supplies the Durango district’s response to the consular census of Japanese residents and recent immigrants.
subfiles.summary: Eaton responds to Consulate General Circular No. 15, which requested statistics on Japanese residents and immigration during the preceding two years. Information supplied by a local Japanese resident indicated that only three Japanese lived in the district and that none had arrived during that period.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on rumors of 100,000 Japanese in Mexico
subfiles.about: Contrasts Washington rumors of 100,000 Japanese in Mexico with the Consulate General’s estimate of slightly more than 5,000.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that rumors circulating in Washington prompted the War Department to request a careful consular check. Consul General Stewart’s recently received confidential report estimated the Japanese population at only a little over 5,000, and the writer asks whether Duggan wishes to examine it.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 55: Information for War Department regarding number of Japanese in Mexico (2)
subfiles.doc_type: confidential consular despatch with map and statistical enclosure
subfiles.from: James B. Stewart, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Presents district-by-district estimates, census comparisons, and migration statistics placing Mexico’s Japanese population at about 5,300.
subfiles.summary: Stewart estimates 5,300 Japanese in Mexico, including about 1,650 in Baja California, using independent reports from American consulates, Japanese sources, and Mexican statistics. The district table records particularly large communities around Mexicali, Piedras Negras, Torreón, Veracruz, Mazatlán, and Mexico City, while noting that recent immigration was generally slight. Census and migration data yield a comparable total of approximately 5,000 and show that restrictive visa policies limited new arrivals, especially through Veracruz. The enclosures are a map of American consular districts and a Mexican Office of Social Statistics table defining and enumerating Japanese immigrants, emigrants, visitors, and tourists from 1930 through November 1936.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting Japanese population estimates to the President
subfiles.about: Informs the President that a confidential consular survey found about 5,300 Japanese in Mexico rather than the rumored 100,000.
subfiles.summary: Welles explains that reports of rapidly increasing Japanese immigration, some claiming a total population of 100,000, led the Department to order a confidential survey by the Consul General in Mexico City. He reports estimates of about 5,300 Japanese nationwide and approximately 1,650 in Baja California, adding that the findings have been communicated to the War Department.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 60: Japanese activities in Mexico, especially on the West Coast
subfiles.from: James B. Stewart, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Summarizes reports on Japanese fishing, coastal travel, propaganda, farming plans, and community organization in several Mexican districts.
subfiles.summary: Reports from Guaymas and Mazatlán describe the MINOWA MARU, MINATO MARU, and smaller Japanese fishing vessels, the movements of Japanese company officials, possible construction of docks and cold storage, and suspicions that technically advanced vessels were charting the coast despite uneconomic catches. The despatch recounts a cordial visit by the Japanese Minister and military attaché to Sinaloa, including a banquet attended by Mexican military and civil officials. It also covers Japanese farmers affected by agrarian reform near Mexicali, a proposed colony south of San Luis along the Colorado River, and the dispersed, close-knit Japanese merchant community in the Piedras Negras district. Stewart encloses Keiichi Ito’s El alma del Japón as an example of Japanese propaganda circulated in Mexico.

subfiles.title: Enclosure identification sheet for Despatch No. 60
subfiles.about: Identifies the following item as an enclosure to Despatch No. 60 concerning Japanese activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The sheet carries the decimal-file number and notes that the attached publication accompanied Despatch No. 60. It functions as the archival divider between Stewart’s report and the enclosed book.

subfiles.title: El alma del Japón
subfiles.doc_type: enclosed Spanish-language book and propaganda publication
subfiles.about: A Spanish-language collection of poems and essays presenting an admiring, nationalist defense of Japanese culture, modernization, diplomacy, and imperial policy.
subfiles.summary: The volume combines patriotic verse with essays on Pacific affairs, Japan’s modernization, medicine, education, transportation, industry, social values, women, and the supposed harmony of traditional and modern Japan. Its political articles defend Japanese actions in Manchuria and China, reject predictions of war with the United States, criticize Western immigration restrictions and naval rivalry, and depict Manchukuo as a stabilizing state. Several essays portray the Soviet Union, communism, and Soviet military development in Siberia and the Far East as the chief threats to Asian peace while insisting that Japan is peaceful and defensive. The final pages begin “Las Flores del Campo de Batalla,” an unfinished account of two seventeen-year-old students named Nobuko who volunteered to serve the Japanese naval landing force during the Shanghai fighting.
